Principle: Meter bridge is based on principle of Wheat stone bridge.

Unknown resistance $X=R\left(\frac{\ell}{100-\ell}\right)$ and specific resistance of the material of the given wire, $\rho=\dfrac{X A}{L}=\dfrac{X\left(\pi r^2\right)}{L} \text {, }$$$ where r and  L are the radius and length of the given wire respectively.

  • Set up the meter bridge with RB in the right gap and X in the left gap. Ensure all connections are tight.
  • Introduce a resistance R=2Ω by taking out the plug from RB and close key K.
  • Move the jockey along the meter-bridge wire until the galvanometer shows no deflection. At this point, AB=$l$ and $BC=(100−l)$
  • Swap RB to the left gap and X to the right gap, then repeat steps 2 and 3. This time, BC= $l$ and  AB = $(100-l)$$$
  • Disconnect the unknown resistance wire, stretch it to remove kinks, and measure its length using a meter scale.
  • Measure the diameter of the wire with a screw gauge.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Ohm's Law: According to the Ohm's law, "the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference applied across its ends provided the physical conditions (temperature, dimensions, pressure) of the conductor remains the same.

$\mathrm{V} \propto \mathrm{I} \text { or } \mathrm{V}=\mathrm{RI}$

$\mathrm{R}=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{I}}$

Graph : Using the readings of voltmeter (V) and ammeter (I) draw a graph as straight line best fitting all the points.

$\text { Slope of } V-I \text { curve }=\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}=\tan \theta=R$

Procedure:

  • Draw the circuit diagram as shown in the figure.
  • Note the range, least count, and zero error of the voltmeter and ammeter.
  • Insert the plug in key K, and slide the rheostat contact to the extreme right to minimize the current.
  • Adjust the rheostat, record ammeter and voltmeter readings, then shift the rheostat contact to increase the current. Repeat for 10 observations.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
The potential difference between the terminal of an electric heater is 60 V when it draws a current of 4 A from the source. What current will the heater draw if the potential difference is changed to 127.5 V ?

(1) 8.5 A

(2) 24 A

(3) 10 A

(4) 12 A
blocks.answer:
(1)8.5A

$\begin{aligned} V & =i R \\ \mathrm{R} & =\frac{60}{4}=15 \Omega \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text { Again } V=i R \\ & i=\frac{V}{R}=\frac{127.5}{15}=8.5 \mathrm{~A} \end{aligned}$

blocks.question:
When a piece of aluminium wire of finite length is drawn to reduce its diameter to half its original value, its resistance will become :-

(1) two times

(2) four times

(3) eight times

(4) sixteen times
blocks.answer:
(4) Sixteen Times

$\begin{aligned} & \text { Initial volume }=\text { final volume } \\ & \frac{\pi d^2 \ell}{4}=\frac{\pi d^2 \mathrm{~L}}{16} \quad \rightarrow\mathrm{~L}=4 \ell, \quad \mathrm{~A}_{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{\mathrm{A}_i}{4} \end{aligned}$

$\displaystyle \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{i}}=\frac{\rho \ell}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{i}}}$

$\displaystyle R_f=\rho\left(\frac{L}{A_f}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{\rho(4 l)}{\left(A_i / 4\right)}$

$\displaystyle R_f=16\left(\frac{\rho l}{A_i}\right) \Rightarrow R_f=16 R_i$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Resistance of galvanometer by half deflection method : When a high resistance R is applied in the circuit with $\mathrm{K}_1$  closed and  $\mathrm{K}_2$ open, the galvanometer draws a current $\mathrm{I}_g$ and shows a deflection  $\theta$  such that

$I_g=\frac{E}{R+G}$

where E, is emf of the battery and G is resistance of the galvanometer. Now $\mathrm{K}_2$ is closed. Adjust the resistance in LRB such that galvanometer deflection becomes equal to $\frac{\theta}{2} .$Now the galvanometer draw the current.

$\displaystyle \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{g}}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{IS}}{\mathrm{G}+\mathrm{S}}=\frac{\mathrm{ES}}{\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{G}+\mathrm{S})+\mathrm{GS}} \quad\left(\text { where } \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{R}+\frac{\mathrm{GS}}{\mathrm{~G+S}}}\right)$

$I_g^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2} I_g$

$\frac{\mathrm{ES}}{\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{G}+\mathrm{S})+\mathrm{GS}}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{G}}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { gives }\\ &\mathrm{G}=\frac{\mathrm{RS}}{\mathrm{R}-\mathrm{S}} \end{aligned}$

Knowing R and S, G can be calculated. Also if R >> S, S can be dropped in comparison to R and then $\mathrm{G} = \mathrm{~S}$

Figure of Merit(Galvanometer)

Figure of merit of galvanometer: It  is defined as the current required per division of deflection in galvanometer. It is denoted by k.

$\text { Figure merit } k=\frac{I}{\theta}$

The circuit diagram for determination of figure of merit (k) of a galvanometer is shown in the figure. When a high resistance R is introduced in the circuit through HRB, a small current $\mathrm{Ig}$ is drawn by it and it shows a deflection $\theta$.

$\displaystyle \mathbf{I}_g=\mathbf{k} \theta=\frac{\mathbf{E}}{\mathbf{R}+\mathbf{G}}$........(1)

$\displaystyle \text { Figure of merit } k=\frac{1}{\theta} \times\left(\frac{E}{R+G}\right)$.........(2)

Maximum current measured by galvanometer or full scale deflection current for galvanometer Ig = Number of division on one side of galvanometer scale × figure of merit

$\begin{aligned} &\text { From equation (ii) }\\ &\frac{1}{\theta}=\frac{k}{E} R+\frac{k}{E} G \end{aligned}$

Graph between  $ \dfrac{1}{\theta} $ and R is as shown.

Procedure:

1.Insert a high resistance Rin HRB and close key $\mathrm{K}_1$  Adjust R to get the deflection $\theta $ in even divisions

2.Close key $\mathrm{K}_2$ and adjust the shunt resistance S from the low resistance box (LRB) to get a deflection half of the previous galvanometer reading.

3.Repeat the experiment for different values of R and $\theta.$

blocks.text:
Process:

  • Draw Line XY: Mark a straight line XY near the center of the sheet, parallel to its length. Mark points O at suitable intervals along this line.
  • Draw Normals: Draw normals to line XY at each point O.
  • Incident Rays: Draw incident rays PQ at angles 30°, 40°, 50°, and 60° using a protractor.
  • Place Prism: Position the prism with one refracting surface on line XY and trace its boundary (ABC).
  • Pin Observations: Place pins P and Q about 8 cm apart on the incident ray and view their images through the prism. Mark pin pricks for images of P, Q, R, and S.
  • Draw Emergent Ray: Join points S and R. Extend the line backward to meet the incident ray PQ.
  • Measure Deviation: Measure the angle of deviation δ and repeat the procedure for different angles of incidence.
  • Angle of Refraction: Mark points O, E, and F on line XY, and draw vertical lines EG, OI, and FH.
  • Prism Placement: Place the prism on the line OI, ensuring its refracting edge aligns with XY. Draw the boundary ABC.
  • Reflection: Fix pins $P_1$  and  $P_2$ observe their reflection, and fix pin $P_3$ Ensure images of pins  $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ are in a straight line. Fix pin P4 on the same line.
  • Join Reflected Ray: Join pricks of $P_3$ and $P_4$ to form line LK. Extend LK backward to find the reflected ray.
  • Measure Angle LPN: Measure angle LPN and determine angle of the prism (∠A).

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: A ray of light passing through an equilateral triangular glass prism from air undergoes minimum deviation when angle of incidence is 3/4th of the angle of prism. Calculate the speed of light in the prism.
blocks.answer:
$i=\frac{3}{4} \mathrm{~A} \quad \text { where }\left\{\begin{array}{l} i=\text { angle of incidence } \\ \mathrm{A}=\text { angle of prism } \end{array}\right.$

$\begin{aligned} &\mu=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin \frac{A}{2}}\\ &\text { ...where }\left[\delta_m=\right.\text { angle of minimum deviation } \end{aligned}$

$\frac{C_1}{C_2}=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{A}+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin \frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}}$

$\delta_m=2 i-\mathrm{A}=2 \times \frac{3}{4} \mathrm{~A}-\mathrm{A}=\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}$

$\delta_m=\frac{60^{\circ}}{2}=30^{\circ} . \Rightarrow \frac{C_1}{C_2}=\frac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{\sin 30^{\circ}}=\sqrt{2}$

$C_2=\frac{3 \times 10^8}{\sqrt{2}} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}=1.5 \sqrt{2} \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

$C_2=2.12 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

blocks.text:
Travelling Microscope: It is a compound microscope fitted vertically on a vertical scale. It can be moved up and down. It consist of a vernier scale moving along the main scale. The reading is taken by combining the main scale and vernier scale reading.

Procedure:

  • Determine the least count by noting the number of Vernier scale divisions (V.S.D.) coinciding with main scale divisions (M.S.D.). Use the formula: Least Count = 1 M.S.D. – 1 V.S.D..
  • Mount the microscope on a stand allowing vertical movement using the rack and pinion.
  • Focus the microscope on a cross mark on paper, noting the reading as  $\mathbf{r}_1$
  • .Place a glass slab on the cross mark, causing it to appear raised.
  • Move the microscope up gently to focus on the cross, recording the reading as $\mathbf{r}_2$
  • Sprinkle powder on the glass slab and move the microscope up until the powder is in focus, recording the reading as $\mathbf{r}_3$
  • For determination of refractive index, by measuring real and apparent depth, a travelling microscope is used. If the reading microscope when focussed on ink mark on white paper r1, reading when the slab is kept over $\mathrm{r}_2$ the ink mark is and the reading of image of lycopodium powder then real depth $=\mathrm{r}_3-\mathrm{r}_1$ and apparent depth$=r_3-r_2$
Therefore refractive index of the material of slog  $\mu=\frac{r_3-r_1}{r_3-r_2}$ $ = \frac{{\operatorname{Real}\,depth}}{{Apparant\,depth}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
P-N Junction Diode :

Forward Bias:

  • As voltage increases from 0V, current rises sharply after reaching the knee (cut-in) voltage.
  • At the knee voltage, barrier potential is eliminated, and diode offers low resistance.
Reverse Bias:

• Reverse current is very small and almost constant (reverse saturation current), indicating high resistance.
    • When reverse voltage reaches breakdown voltage (VB), current increases sharply due to avalanche breakdown.

rows: Order of forward current is milliampere.
Order of current is micro ampere (Ge) or Nano ampere (Si).
Current flows mainly due to majority charge carrier.
Current flows mainly due to minority charge carrier.

• Switch should be used only when the circuit is being used.

• Reverse bias voltage beyond breakdown should not be applied.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Zener Diode: It is a special purpose diode, designed to operate under the reverse bias in the breakdown region and used in voltage regulation.

Symbol of Zener diode:

In reverse bias of Zener diode after the breakdown voltage  $V_z$, a large change in the current can be produced by very small change in the reverse bias voltage. In other words zener voltage remains constant, even though current through the zener diode varies over a wide range. This property of the zener diode is used for regulating voltage.

The circuit diagram for plotting the characteristics of a Zener diode and determine its reverse breakdown voltage

Zener Diode Across Load

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{I}}=\text { Input voltage } \\ & \mathrm{V}_0=\text { Output voltage } \\ & \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}}=\text { Input resistance } \\ & \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{L}}=\text { Load resistance } \\ & \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{1}}=\text { Input current } \\ & \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{Z}}=\text { Zener diode current } \\ & \mathrm{I} \mathrm{~L}=\text { Load current } \end{aligned}$

Relations :

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{1}}-\mathrm{Iz} \\ & \mathrm{~V}_0=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{I}}-\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{I}} \\ & \mathrm{~V}_0=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{L}} \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{L}} \end{aligned}$

Initially as $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{I}}$ is increased,  $\mathrm{I}_1$ increases a little, then $\mathrm{V}_0$ increases. At breakdown, increase of $V_1 $ increases $ I_1$by large amount, so that

$$$\mathrm{V}_0=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{I}}-\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{I}} \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{I}}$  $\text { becomes constant. }$

This constant value of $\mathrm{V}_0$ which is the reverse breakdown voltage is called Zener voltage.$$

rows: Where covalent bonds of depletion layer, itself break, due to high electric field of Reverse bias voltage.
Here covalent bonds of depletion layer are broken by collision of "Minorities" which acquire high kinetic energy from high electric field of very-very high reverse bias voltage.
This phenomena takes place in(i) P – N junction having "High doping"(ii) P – N junction having thin depletion layer
This phenomena takes place in(i) P – N junction having "Low doping"(ii) P – N junction having thick depletion layer
Here P – N junction does not damage permanently. "In D.C voltage stabilizer zener phenomena is used".
Here P – N junction damages permanently due to abruptly increment of minorities during repetitive collisions.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Diodes: In some semiconductor diodes, a silver ring on one end indicates the n-side, while the p-side is at the opposite end. In diodes with painted symbols, the arrow points in the direction of the forward bias current, with the p-side at the arrow's base and the n-side at its tip. Bullet-shaped diodes have a flat side as the p-side and a cylindrical side as the n-side.

  • A diode is a two terminal device. It conducts when forward biased and does not conduct when reverse biased.
  • It does not emit light while conducting.
  • If the multimeter does not show any deflection in one direction and shows deflection with no light emission in the other direction then, the component is a diode.
  • Light emitting diode: A LED (light emitting diode) is also a two terminal device. It conducts when forward biased and does not conduct when reverse biased. It emits light while conducting. In case of a light emitting diode (LED), usually the shorter pin is n-side and the longer pin is p-side
If the deflection is accompanied with emission of light, in one direction and a much less or zero deflection in the other direction the component is a LED.

Resistor: A resistor is a two terminal device. It conducts equally in both directions. Look for colour bands, if it has a typical set of three colour bands followed by a silver or gold band, the component is a resistor.If the multimeter showns an equal deflection in both the directions, the component is a resistor.

Colour code for resistor: Most common colour code used for resistor consists of three colour bands at one end.

The colour and their numerical meanings are:

Black – 0          Orange – 3                 Blue – 6                     White – 9

Brown – 1         Yellow – 4                    Violet – 7

Red – 2              Green – 5                     Grey – 8

  • This colour code could be remembered easily by the term BBROY GB VGW (B B ROY Great Britain Very Good Wife). To read the resistance of a colour coded resistor, start with the strip nearest to the end. The colour of the first strip gives the first digit in the resistance value. The colour of the second strip stands for the second digit. The colour of third strip indicates the value of multiplier or the number of zero following second number
$\begin{aligned} &\text { Resistance for the given resistor }\\ &$$\begin{aligned} & =27 \times 10^3 \pm 10 \% \text { of } 27 \times 10^3 \\ & =(27 \pm 2.7) \times 10^3 \Omega \end{aligned}$$ \end{aligned}$$

Resistors with only three bands have a tolerance of 20%. Its actual value may vary 20% up or down from its indicated value. If a fourth band is added separated from the first three, then the tolerance of the resistor is known from the colour of the fourth band. If the colour of the fourth band is silver, then tolerance is 10%.Gold colour represents 5% tolerance red represents 2% and brown represents 1%.

Capacitor: It is a device that stores electrical charge. A capacitor blocks the passage of dc while it allows ac to flow through it.

There are many types of capacitors having different types of dielectrics in general use. These are

(i) Air capacitor (variable gang capacitors)

(ii) Mica capacitor (low capacitance)

(iii) Ceramic capacitor (very low capacitance)

(iv) Paper capacitor (low capacitance)

(v) Plastic capacitor

(vi) Electrolytic capacitor (medium capacitance)

(vii) Oil filled capacitor (high capacitance)

A capacitor is a two terminal device. It does not conduct but stores some charge when dc voltage is applied. If the multimeter does not show any deflection on connecting its terminals either way to the component, it is a capacitor. But if capacitance of capacitor is large, multimeter may show a momentary deflection.

rows: Initially very high which eventually decays to zero

  • Lift the jockey while moving to locate the balance point, do not slide it on the wire.
  • Insert the plug in key K only when taking observations.
  • The balance point should be between 30 cm and 70 cm.
  • Measure the wire's diameter in two perpendicular directions at one spot.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Ensure neat, clean, and tight connections.
    • Use thick copper wires for connections.
    • Select appropriate range for voltmeter and ammeter.
    • Insert the key/plug only during observations to avoid unnecessary heating.
    • Ensure the unknown resistance is not lower than the battery’s internal resistance.
    • Connect ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel with the resistor.
    • Eliminate zero error in voltmeter and ammeter before taking observations.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Ensure all circuit connections are neat, clean, and tight.
    • Tighten all plugs in HRB and LRB.
    • Introduce high resistance RR first, then close key  $K_1$ to prevent overcurrent.

• Ensure constant emf from the cell/battery.
    • Aim for maximum galvanometer deflection with even divisions.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Fix Pins Vertically: Ensure all pins are fixed vertically.
    • Use Sharp Pencil: Use a sharp pencil for drawing the prism boundary and making pin pricks.
    • Angle of Incidence: Set the angle of incidence between 30° and 60°.
    • Mark Arrow Heads: Add arrowheads to indicate the direction of incident and emergent rays.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Microscope should be focused properly and reading should be taken carefully.
    • Extremely small amount of powder should be used.
    • Microscope may not be focused well.
    • It may have faulty calibration.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• All connections should be clean and tight

• Switch should be used only when the circuit is being used.

• Reverse bias voltage beyond breakdown should not be applied.

    • Switch should be used only when the circuit is being used.
    • Zero reading of voltmeter and micro ammeter should be checked properly.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Mistaking the polarity can cause the LED to not light up or even get damaged.
  • Electrolytic capacitors are polarized, so reversing their connections can damage them.
  • Resistor color codes can be difficult to read or misinterpreted, leading to wrong resistance values.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Resistance of galvanometer by half deflection method : When a high resistance R is applied in the circuit with $\mathrm{K}_1$  closed and  $\mathrm{K}_2$ open, the galvanometer draws a current $\mathrm{I}_g$ and shows a deflection  $\theta$  such that

$I_g=\frac{E}{R+G}$

where E, is emf of the battery and G is resistance of the galvanometer. Now $\mathrm{K}_2$ is closed. Adjust the resistance in LRB such that galvanometer deflection becomes equal to $\frac{\theta}{2} .$Now the galvanometer draw the current.

$\displaystyle \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{g}}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{IS}}{\mathrm{G}+\mathrm{S}}=\frac{\mathrm{ES}}{\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{G}+\mathrm{S})+\mathrm{GS}} \quad\left(\text { where } \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{R}+\frac{\mathrm{GS}}{\mathrm{~G+S}}}\right)$

$I_g^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2} I_g$

$\frac{\mathrm{ES}}{\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{G}+\mathrm{S})+\mathrm{GS}}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{G}}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { gives }\\ &\mathrm{G}=\frac{\mathrm{RS}}{\mathrm{R}-\mathrm{S}} \end{aligned}$

Knowing R and S, G can be calculated. Also if R >> S, S can be dropped in comparison to R and then $\mathrm{G} = \mathrm{~S}$

Figure of Merit(Galvanometer)

Figure of merit of galvanometer: It  is defined as the current required per division of deflection in galvanometer. It is denoted by k.

$\text { Figure merit } k=\frac{I}{\theta}$

The circuit diagram for determination of figure of merit (k) of a galvanometer is shown in the figure. When a high resistance R is introduced in the circuit through HRB, a small current $\mathrm{Ig}$ is drawn by it and it shows a deflection $\theta$.

$\displaystyle \mathbf{I}_g=\mathbf{k} \theta=\frac{\mathbf{E}}{\mathbf{R}+\mathbf{G}}$........(1)

$\displaystyle \text { Figure of merit } k=\frac{1}{\theta} \times\left(\frac{E}{R+G}\right)$.........(2)

Maximum current measured by galvanometer or full scale deflection current for galvanometer Ig = Number of division on one side of galvanometer scale × figure of merit

$\begin{aligned} &\text { From equation (ii) }\\ &\frac{1}{\theta}=\frac{k}{E} R+\frac{k}{E} G \end{aligned}$

Graph between  $ \dfrac{1}{\theta} $ and R is as shown.

Procedure:

1.Insert a high resistance Rin HRB and close key $\mathrm{K}_1$  Adjust R to get the deflection $\theta $ in even divisions

2.Close key $\mathrm{K}_2$ and adjust the shunt resistance S from the low resistance box (LRB) to get a deflection half of the previous galvanometer reading.

3.Repeat the experiment for different values of R and $\theta.$
